briefing.opening: Good day. We begin the Climate Daily Briefing for November 24, 2026.

sections.title: 🔴 Collapse of Antalya COP31 Agreement and the Deadlock of Multilateral Climate Diplomacy
sections.content: The 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31), held in Antalya, Türkiye, ended in failure without adopting a final agreement amid staunch opposition to fossil fuel language from countries including Saudi Arabia [3, 4, 110, 123]. At this summit, key sticking points included not only the clash between oil-producing nations and the international community over phasing out fossil fuels, but also the practical limitations of carbon capture technologies [112, 118]. Furthermore, while climate adaptation requires $305 billion annually, international support stands at barely one-tenth of that figure, repeatedly exposing structural flaws in the global climate finance system [6, 109]. Following the summit's collapse, the European Union (EU) has officially moved to pursue a comprehensive overhaul of the existing UN climate negotiation process [113].

sections.title: ⚠️ Record Heatwave Deaths and Accelerating Global Extreme Weather
sections.content: As deadly floods, wildfires, and droughts continue unabated, the human toll of climate change is becoming increasingly visible [92, 106, 121]. In the United Kingdom, summer heatwave deaths in England reached 5,258 between May and September 2026, marking an all-time high since statistics began a decade ago [119]. Dry, hot winds are worsening across China's wheat belt [82], while in Rwanda, warming-induced increases in mosquito populations have caused a surge in malaria cases, deepening the climate-health crisis [97]. South Korea is also witnessing pronounced weather extremes driven by climate change, with the intensity and frequency of torrential rains increasing sharply due to higher atmospheric moisture and prolonged weather stagnation [1].

sections.title: ⚠️ Surging AI Power Demand and Practical Barriers to Transition Infrastructure
sections.content: The explosive growth of the artificial intelligence (AI) industry is emerging as a major challenge to carbon reduction policies [22]. Most notably, Meta's data center greenhouse gas emissions surged 12-fold in just one year, putting the company's 2030 net-zero target at risk of being virtually scrapped [41]. As a result, the scientific and technological community has issued consecutive recommendations urging that AI energy demands be tightly integrated into national carbon neutrality strategies [22]. Domestically, however, sluggish budget execution and inadequate electrical grid infrastructure persist despite the push to expand renewable energy [53], while local municipalities in Gyeonggi Province have set emissions reduction targets without securing the necessary financial backing, raising serious doubts about policy implementation [49].

sections.title: 🌱 Advances in Climate Tech Academia-Industry Collaboration and Field-Driven Ecological and Agricultural Adaptation
sections.content: Despite setbacks in international negotiations, tangible climate response momentum continues across regional and technological frontiers [103, 114]. Domestically, the Korea Institute of Climate Change and Hallym University have launched efforts to strengthen technology-based resilience by establishing a Climate Tech Innovation Center and initiating research-industry partnerships [2, 5, 8, 11]. In the fields of ecology and agriculture, a joint research team from the Jeju World Natural Heritage Center and Seoul National University sequenced the world's first genome map of the endangered Hallasan Korean fir [75]. Tailored adaptation technologies are also yielding results, including the successful cultivation of tangerines in Pocheon using geothermal heat and the demonstration of 'RE100 tangerines' powered by greenhouse solar panels [16, 74]. Furthermore, distributed energy expansion is gaining traction, with private enterprises developing 1 GW-scale rooftop solar projects and local governments passing renewable energy support ordinances [50, 59].

briefing.closing: Even amid the deadlock in multilateral negotiations and the acceleration of climate disasters, on-the-ground and technology-driven climate adaptation efforts continue to advance steadily. That concludes today's climate briefing.
